product.title: Hindi 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Hindi: the pronunciation is printed right above every Devanagari word, with short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Hindi builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a full Devanagari chart with vowel signs, a guide to retroflex and aspirated sounds, a page of Perso-Arabic words with a familiar ring, a summary of A1 verb forms, and a glossary. Written for English speakers — each unit targets one point that most often trips learners up, from verbs that change with the speaker's gender to the little ने that shifts the subject of a sentence once the story moves into the past.

blocks.text: Hindi has an unfair reputation. People open the first page, see a row of letters hanging from a line like जन्मदिन, and close the book again. Yet the Devanagari script is the **most honest** part of this whole journey. One letter, one sound, and that sound never shifts depending on its neighbors. Once you know the sounds of its fifty-odd letters, you can read any Hindi word correctly — including words you've never seen in your life. Compare that with English, where *though*, *through*, *tough*, and *thought* use the same letters for four different sounds.

The real difficulties are in three other places, and this course won't pretend otherwise. First, **every noun has a gender** — masculine or feminine — and English has nothing like it. Second, and most surprising, **verbs follow the gender of the speaker**. A man says मैं जाता हूँ, a woman says मैं जाती हूँ, and both mean "I go". You'll use that form in your very first sentence, so unit 4 covers it thoroughly. Third, **the Hindi verb stands at the end of the sentence**. मैं हिंदी बोलता हूँ, word for word, is "I — Hindi — speaking — am". It sounds backwards in week one; by week three it sounds normal.

The good news is far greater than people expect. Hindi has no articles — no *the*, no *a*. घर means "house", "a house", and "the house" all at once. Verbs have no irregular present tense to memorize: one pattern serves nearly every verb. Most of the sounds exist in English, and the ones that don't are easy to copy because you've heard them in songs and films. And a question is formed just by putting क्या in front — no inversion, no *do*.

There's one more gift, and it's closer to home than you'd think: **you already know some Hindi words**. English borrowed them during centuries of contact: *jungle* is जंगल, *bungalow* is बंगला, *pyjamas* is पाजामा, *loot* is लूट, *thug* is ठग, *chutney* is चटनी, *shampoo* comes from चाँपो ("press!"), and *guru*, *karma*, and *yoga* are Hindi words too. Hindi also carries a large layer of Persian and Arabic words — वक़्त, ख़बर, जवाब, सवाल, मुश्किल, उम्र, हवा, माफ़, शुक्रिया, मौसम — shared with Urdu, Persian, Turkish, Swahili, and Malay. A special page in this book collects them.

Three things are deliberately done differently from most Hindi textbooks. First, **the pronunciation is printed right above each Hindi word**, not on a separate line, so your eyes don't jump back and forth and lose their place mid-sentence. This isn't decoration: Hindi swallows the letter *a* in many places — नाम is said *naam*, not *naama*; घर is *ghar*, not *ghara* — and without the reading above it, beginners memorize the wrong sound for months. Second, every line of dialogue has a **word-for-word translation** that shows the original order, even when that order sounds odd — because that's exactly where the lesson is. Third, each unit targets **one typical stumbling point for English speakers**, and it's named openly, not hidden in a footnote.

One last thing. Six hundred million people speak Hindi, and it has a near-identical twin — Urdu — so what you learn here carries from Delhi to Lahore, from Mumbai to Karachi, and to every corner of the world that watches Indian films. Say one Hindi sentence to an Indian you meet and see for yourself what happens to their face. That's your first reward, and it comes much sooner than you think.

This course is designed for self-study, without a teacher, twenty to thirty minutes per sitting. One unit = one sitting. Don't do two units at once, however easy it feels — Hindi builds up in layers, and a unit done in a hurry will send you the bill in unit 14.
Suggested order within a unit

items: **Read the title and the "by the end" list.** Those five lines are the unit's promise. If at the end you can do all five without looking, the unit is done.

**Read the dialogue aloud, twice.** Once looking at the pronunciation above the letters, once more covering the pronunciation with your finger and trying to read the Devanagari directly. That second round is what teaches the script — not the alphabet chart.
**Only then read the translation.** Reversing this order is the most common mistake: if you read the meaning first, your eyes never truly look at the Hindi sentence.
**Pay attention to the literal line.** The small line under each sentence shows the original Hindi word order. That's where you learn to think in Hindi rather than translate from English.
**Do the exercises by hand, on paper.** Answering in your head feels faster and works far worse. The answer key is on the same page, so cover it with paper first.

front.title: Devanagari: a script that hangs from a line

blocks.text: Devanagari is written differently from the Latin alphabet, and once you see how, the letters stop looking like a fence. Picture a rope stretched out horizontally. The letters **hang below the rope**, rather than sitting on a line like Latin letters. The rope is called **शिरोरेखा** (*shi-ro-re-khaa*, "head line"), and it runs unbroken along a whole word. That's what makes it useful: **a break in the head line marks the boundary between words**, just as a space does for us.

The second thing to know: **every consonant letter already carries an *a* sound**. क isn't "k" but "ka". म isn't "m" but "ma". So कम is read *kam*, and कमल is read *ka-mal*. You don't write the vowel *a* — it's there from the start.
Other vowels are attached as a **matra**, a small stroke stuck to the right, left, top, or bottom of the letter. Watch the letter क below change its sound purely through its stroke:

blocks.title: Three small marks that change the reading
items: **ं (bindu)** and **ँ (chandrabindu)** — nasal sound. हैं is read *haiⁿ*, नहीं is read *na-hiiⁿ*. The air goes out through the nose while the mouth stays open. Before a consonant it becomes an ordinary n or m: हिंदी = *hin-dii*, संवाद = *sam-vaad*.

**् (halant/virama)** — a small stroke under a letter that **removes its *a* sound**. क् is a bare "k". In everyday writing it more often shows up as a conjunct letter: क + ् + या becomes **क्या** (*kyaa*, what).

**़ (nuqta)** — a small dot under a letter, marking a sound borrowed from Persian and Arabic. ज → ज़ (*z*), फ → फ़ (*f*), क → क़ (*q*). Notice: almost every word with a nuqta is a Perso-Arabic loan — ज़रूरी, फ़ायदा, क़िस्मत (*kismet*!), वक़्त.

blocks.text: Finally, don't worry about **conjunct letters** (संयुक्ताक्षर) in the first weeks. When two consonants meet with no vowel between them, they merge into one new shape: क + ष = क्ष, त + र = त्र, ज + ञ = ज्ञ. Their shapes do have to be learned one by one, but fewer than twenty are really common, and the pronunciation above each word will guide you until you recognize them yourself.

The order is the official one — the same as in a Hindi dictionary. It isn't random like the Latin alphabet but arranged by **where the tongue goes**: from the back of the throat moving forward to the lips. The "Pronunciation" column shows the symbols used throughout this course.

blocks.text: ⚠️ In everyday writing — shop signs, newspapers, WhatsApp messages — **the nuqta is often left out**. ज़रूरी becomes जरूरी, फ़ोन becomes फोन. The sound is still *z* and *f*; only the dot is missing. This course writes the nuqta so you learn the right sound, but don't be surprised when it vanishes in the street.

front.title: Retroflex sounds, aspirated sounds, and the vanishing a

blocks.text: The three things on these pages are all the real sound difficulties Hindi holds for an English speaker. Master them and the rest flows on its own.
1. Retroflex sounds (ट ठ ड ढ ण ड़)

Hindi has **two different series of t and d**, and the difference changes meaning. For the first series (त थ द ध न), the tip of the tongue touches **the back of the upper front teeth** — further forward than English t. For the second (ट ठ ड ढ ण), the tip of the tongue **curls back** and touches the roof of the mouth. It sounds more hollow. English t and d sit in between, and Indians usually hear them as the retroflex series. In this course the retroflex series is **always written with capitals** in the pronunciation: T, Th, D, Dh, N, R.

blocks.title: ⚠️ What this means for the pronunciation in this course
items: **A capital letter in the pronunciation never means the start of a sentence or a name.** It always and only means a retroflex sound. That's why even names are written in lower case: दिल्ली becomes *dil-lii*, राम becomes *raam*.

If you really can't hear the difference in week one, use your ordinary English t and d and keep going. Indians will still understand you. But start noticing it now, because an ear that knows the difference begins to hear it on its own.

blocks.text: 2. Aspirated sounds (ख घ छ झ ठ ढ थ ध फ भ)

An aspirated sound is an ordinary consonant released with **a puff of breath**. The difference is clear and changes meaning — it's not decoration. To test it, hold your palm ten centimeters in front of your mouth. Say **कल** (*kal*, yesterday) — your palm should feel nothing. Then say **खाल** (*khaal*, skin) — your palm should feel one short puff. ⚠️ English speakers have the opposite problem from most learners: you already put a puff on k, p, and t at the start of words (*kill*, *pin*, *top*), so the hard part is the **unaspirated** sound. Say it like the k in *skill* or the p in *spin*.

⚠️ Note that **ph is an aspirated p, not f**, and **th is an aspirated t, not the English *th***. थोड़ा is read *tho-Raa* with an aspirated t — not as in *think*. Likewise **chh** is just ch with a strong puff. This is the near-universal mistake of learners who read Hindi through English spelling; now you can avoid it.
3. The vanishing a

This is the main reason this course prints the pronunciation **above** each word. Every Devanagari consonant carries an *a* sound, but modern Hindi **drops that *a* at the end of a word, and often in the middle too**. The rules are real but layered, and there's no point memorizing them at the start — all you need to do is trust the printed pronunciation.

The last two rows show something subtler still: when **ह** is squeezed in the middle, the vowels around it change color toward *e*. That's why बहन sounds like *be-han*, and बहुत sounds like *ba-hut* with a faint a. Again — don't memorize it, just read what's printed aloud, and your mouth will learn by itself.

front.title: Hindi words with a familiar ring

blocks.text: For centuries Persian was the court language of northern India, and through it Hindi absorbed a wave of Persian and Arabic words. The same wave reached Urdu, Turkish, Swahili, and Malay — and a few of these words even made it into English. Here are fifty everyday ones. Several will ring a bell; the rest are worth learning as a set, because they share sounds (q, kh, gh, z, f) and many share the same feminine gender.

blocks.title: Three warnings before you get too excited
items: ⚠️ **Some words are used more widely than you'd expect.** मुश्किल ("difficult") is used every day for anything hard, and हाल ("state") turns up in an everyday greeting: *आपका हाल कैसा है?* — "how are you doing?"

⚠️ **Some sound alike but aren't related.** कमरा (*kam-raa*) means "room" — from Portuguese *câmara*, a cousin of English *chamber*. But आम means "mango" **and** "common", and कल means "yesterday" **and** "tomorrow" (unit 13 explains).

⚠️ **There's a second layer of words with no familiar ring**: the native Sanskrit-derived words such as पानी, आदमी, लड़का, बहन, घर, खाना. These are the ones used most. So don't expect to guess whole sentences — treat the Perso-Arabic words as a bonus that pops up a few times per page.

blocks.text: A short historical note that explains it all: Hindi and Urdu are essentially **the same language** in everyday conversation, with two different scripts and two different stores of literary vocabulary. Urdu takes its learned words from Persian and Arabic; Hindi takes them from Sanskrit. Street conversation uses both without choosing. That means this course also takes you a good way into Urdu — and into the language of almost every Indian film song you've ever heard.

back.title: Nouns: gender, plural, and the oblique form

blocks.text: This one page sums up every noun change you need at A1. If there's one page worth photographing and keeping on your phone, it's this one.
Four groups of nouns

blocks.title: When the oblique form is used
items: **Always, and only, when a postposition follows**: में, पर, से, को, का/की/के, तक, के पास, के लिए.
⚠️ **The oblique plural always ends in -ों, no exceptions** — even for feminine nouns. It's the one truly tidy part of this system; hold on to it.
⚠️ Masculine nouns that **don't** end in -आ don't change at all in the oblique singular: घर में, घर पर, घर से. Many beginners think something must change; nothing does.

blocks.text: Adjectives follow their noun
Only adjectives ending in **-आ** change. The rest (सुंदर, ख़ूबसूरत, ठीक, ज़रूरी, मुश्किल, साफ़) never change at all.

6. Future — "will"
Stem + **ऊँगा/ऊँगी** (I), **एगा/एगी** (he/she), **ओगे** (तुम), **एँगे/एँगी** (we, you polite, they). मैं जाऊँगा · मैं जाऊँगी · वह जाएगा · तुम जाओगे · हम जाएँगे · आप जाएँगे.
Commands at three levels
Prohibitions: **मत** for commands (मत जाओ — don't go), **न** for gentle requests (न जाइए). ⚠️ नहीं is for negating statements, not for forbidding.

Hindi numbers can't be built from parts the way English ones can. **Each of the first hundred is its own word**, and there's no shortcut. You can do two things: learn 1–20 and the round tens first, then notice that the rest always follow the pattern "unit stuck in front of the next ten" — इक·तीस (31), पैं·तालीस (45), छि·हत्तर (76).

Above a hundred: **सौ** (100), **हज़ार** (1,000), **लाख** (100,000), **करोड़** (10,000,000). ⚠️ India counts in **lakh** and **crore**, not millions — दो लाख = 200,000, and एक करोड़ = ten million. You'll meet both in house prices, salaries, and the news, so get used to them now.
Clock time

**साढ़े तीन means 3:30** — just like English *half past three*: Hindi names the hour that has *already passed*. ⚠️ If you know German or Dutch, beware: there *halb vier* is 3:30, and the habit can follow you into Hindi.

blocks.text: Dates put the number first, then the month, as in British English: **१५ अगस्त** — पंद्रह अगस्त (15 August). Devanagari numerals (१२३४५६७८९०) still appear on signs and banknotes, but Western numerals are far more common in everyday writing.

blocks.title: Two habits that make your questions sound natural
items: **क्या at the start of a sentence = yes/no question marker**, and it isn't translated. क्या आप हिंदी बोलते हैं? = "Do you speak Hindi?" Compare क्या in the middle of a sentence, where it means "what": आप क्या बोलते हैं?

⚠️ **The question word goes right before the verb**, not at the start of the sentence as in English. आप **कहाँ** जा रहे हैं? — not *कहाँ आप जा रहे हैं?*. It seems minor, but it's what most quickly makes your sentences sound like real Hindi.

blocks.text: Words that appear in this course, arranged in English alphabetical order. **(f)** marks a feminine noun, **(m)** a masculine one — learn the gender together with the word, because it can't be guessed from the meaning.

If you've reached this page after working through all twenty units, you're now at a genuine A1 level: you can introduce yourself, shop, order food, ask for directions, talk about days gone by and days to come, and turn down an invitation without offending anyone. That's no small thing. What follows is how to turn it into a skill that doesn't evaporate.
The next four weeks

items: **Week 1 — consolidate what you have.** Redo the exercises of units 1–10 without your notes. Where you get stuck marks a unit to reread, not a unit you failed.

**Week 2 — move it to your ears.** Find a short Indian series with Hindi subtitles (not English) and watch one episode again and again until you can guess lines before they're said. One episode five times beats five episodes once.
**Week 3 — move it to your hands.** Write five sentences about your day, every day, in Devanagari. Five sentences, not fifty. Consistency is what works.

**Week 4 — move it to your mouth.** Find one conversation partner: a private tutor, a language-exchange friend, or anyone in the Indian community in your city. Thirty minutes of speaking beats three hours of reading.

blocks.title: Three truly useful resources
items: **Film songs.** Hindi film lyrics are written to be understood all over India, so the vocabulary is simple and repetitive. Look up the lyrics in Devanagari, not Latin transliteration — it's reading practice that doesn't feel like practice.

**Children's stories and picture books.** Publishers such as *Pratham Books* offer beginner-level Hindi picture stories for free. The sentences are short and the vocabulary is right within your reach now.

**Signs and packaging.** If you get the chance to visit India, reading shop signs aloud is the fastest way to turn the script from "decoded" into "recognized". If not, photos of Indian product packaging at your nearest Indian grocery will do.

blocks.text: One last thing, and it isn't a polite closing line. Hindi pays you back faster than almost any other language, because its speakers rarely meet foreigners who've bothered to learn it. Your first sentence will be met with a warmth that may leave you a little flustered. Just accept it, answer with **शुक्रिया**, and keep going. आपको शुभकामनाएँ — good luck.
